idiom_name: Boost.Asio async_receive completion handler on io_context
implementation_notes: Boost.Asio is the canonical C++ substrate: io_context runs the loop and invokes a completion handler once async_receive (or async_read) has data, so the endpoint never blocks and the handler is the listener. What replaces the classic structure is the completion-handler chain - the consumer object starts a receive, and only the callback runs after delivery; hand-rolled threads around blocking read() are the manual fallback. Choose the plain callback form when the toolchain is pre-C++20 or the code must interoperate with C-style APIs.
pitfalls: A completion handler that blocks (sleep, synchronous I/O, long computation) stalls every other operation on the same io_context thread; offload heavy work or use a thread pool with strands.
The handler must keep the buffer and socket alive until it runs: capturing locals by reference is the classic dangling-completion bug.
async_receive may complete with a partial message; framing and reassembly stay the application's job.
A socket with a pending async_receive keeps io_context.run() alive - cancellation is part of shutdown.

variants.name: Boost.Asio with C++20 coroutines (co_await)
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 stackless coroutines turn the callback chain into linear code: co_spawn runs an awaitable that co_awaits async_receive in a loop, while the io_context still owns delivery - the consumer's state lives in the coroutine frame instead of handler captures. Prefer this form on a C++20 toolchain when the handler nesting hurts readability; completion tokens decide whether errors surface as exceptions or as tuples (as_tuple). The classic callback variant remains right for pre-C++20 code or when handlers must interoperate with C APIs.
pitfalls: Detached co_spawn erases ownership: the coroutine frame must own or outlive the socket, otherwise it resumes on a destroyed connection.
Without as_tuple/redirect_error, transport errors are thrown from co_await; a coroutine that swallows them silently stops consuming.
The coroutine still runs on the io_context executor - blocking inside an awaitable stalls the loop just as it does inside a handler.
